checks.claim: A typical backyard pool holds roughly 15,000 to 20,000 gallons of water.
checks.why: Vita Filters says the average residential pool holds 15,000-20,000 gallons, and Swimming Pool Steve gives 17,280 gallons for a 16'x32' pool. Above-ground pools run smaller, about 13,500 gallons. The sources are industry ones only.

checks.claim: Many in-ground pool shells are gunite or shotcrete, which is concrete sprayed through a hose. Gunite is the dry-mix version and shotcrete the wet-mix version.
checks.why: The sources support the sprayed-concrete description but give no market-share data, so "most" is unsupported. Vinyl-liner and fiberglass in-ground pools also exist.

checks.claim: A residential pool pump is typically sized to turn over the pool's water about once every 6 to 8 hours (some retailers say 8 to 10). Public pools are held to faster turnover, with the CDC Model Aquatic Health Code targeting 6 hours.
checks.why: The 8-hour figure is common but not a single fixed standard. Sources range from 6-8 to 8-10 hours. The 6-hour MAHC figure is secondhand, from AJ Designer.

checks.claim: The strong chlorine smell at pools comes from chloramines, chlorine that has bonded with sweat, urine and oils.
checks.why: The CDC says the chlorine smell is probably chloramines. Industry sources (Mavaquadoc) describe them as forming when chlorine binds to sweat, oils and urine.
